title: Don't lose heart
hookLine: after Uhud: don't weaken or grieve, days of fortune rotate among people (3:139–140)

cards: A year after their first victory at Badr, the Muslims of Medina met a much larger army from Mecca at the foot of a mountain called Uhud. The battle started well.
Then a group of archers, told by the Prophet ﷺ never to leave their hill, saw the enemy running and came down for the spoils. The cavalry swept around behind them.
Many Muslims died, among them the Prophet's uncle Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. They walked home to a city in mourning.

teach.b: A large part of Al 'Imran, from around verse 121, speaks into the days after that loss. It doesn't pretend the defeat didn't happen, or hide the mistake.
But 3:139 says, in Pickthall's words: "Faint not nor grieve." And 3:140 gives a surprising reason. If a wound has touched you, a wound like it touched the other side too, at Badr.
Then: these are the days, and We make them take turns among people. The verb is nudawiluha, from the root d-w-l, to rotate, to pass from hand to hand.

The same root gives dawla, which today means a state, a country, but at heart means a turn: power is something that rotates. So the verse doesn't promise you'll always win. It says the days turn, for everyone.

Good days and bad days are passed around, and neither one stays forever. The verse adds that this is how God makes known who truly believes, and takes witnesses, shuhada, from among them: the martyrs of Uhud.
There's grief in it, and dignity.

And this week built toward it: a chosen family carrying a weight, Zakariyya's silence, Maryam, a common word, the rope, a people who call to good. Now a community knocked down, and told: don't lose heart.

how: Muslims remember Uhud and its martyrs, including Hamzah, the Prophet's uncle, and the verses of Al 'Imran revealed after the battle are often recited for comfort after loss and defeat.

o: We make them take turns, hand to hand
We record them in the book of deeds
We count them until the Last Day

p: left their hill for the spoils

s: the Qur'an hides the defeat at Uhud
a long passage of Al 'Imran speaks openly about the loss and the mistake.
the Arabic for 'take turns' shares a root with dawla
d-w-l: to rotate; dawla, a state, at heart means a turn.
the verse promises believers will always win
it says the days take turns among people.

games.q: you're one of the archers at Uhud. the Prophet told you never to leave the hill. you see the enemy running. what happened?
o: all the archers stayed at their post.
many came down for the spoils, and the cavalry swept around behind.
the archers chased the enemy back to Mecca.
games.why: many left the hill, the enemy cavalry came round behind, and a winning battle turned into a painful loss.

practice: Bring to mind a recent loss or setback, small or large, and feel it honestly; the verse doesn't ask anyone to pretend.
Then remember a day in your past that felt just as bad and has since turned, a day you got through, and breathe with both of them. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Nudawiluha, we make them take turns. Spoken to the Muslims after Uhud: faint not nor grieve, the days take turns among people. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: We make them take turns (3:140), said of the days; root d-w-l, to rotate.

carryVoice: Your line: days turn. Uhud's grief was real, and so was the turning. A week, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Battle of Uhud)
